title: Shared Values Counted From Each Side
statement:
You get two integer arrays, a and b. Return a pair [left, right]:

  • left is the number of positions i in a whose value a[i] appears anywhere in b.
  • right is the number of positions j in b whose value b[j] appears anywhere in a.

Positions are counted, not distinct values: a value that appears three times in a and at least once in b adds 3 to left.

examples.why: In a, the two 4s and the 9 are found in b (3 positions). In b, the 4 and all three 9s are found in a (4 positions).
Counting distinct shared values would give [1, 1]. Each position counts, so the sides differ.

hints: For each position you only need a yes/no: is this value present on the other side?
Rescanning the other array for every position costs O(n·m). What structure answers "is x present?" in O(1)?
Build a set from each array, then count positions of a whose value is in set(b), and positions of b whose value is in set(a).

explain.intuition:
The question for every position is a membership test: does this value exist in the other array? A hash set answers that in O(1), so turn each array into a set once and then walk the other array counting hits.

The trap is the word "positions". Duplicates on one side each count, while duplicates on the other side do not matter at all, because a set only records presence. That is why the two numbers can differ.
pitfalls: Counting distinct shared values instead of positions: [2, 2, 2] vs [2] must give 3 on the left.
Using one shared count for both sides. The answer is asymmetric whenever duplicates differ.
Calling includes inside the loop, which quietly makes it O(n·m).

solutions.title: Scan the other array for each position
solutions.idea: For every element, search the other array linearly.

solutions.title: Two hash sets
solutions.idea: Turn each array into a set once; then every membership check is O(1).

followups: Both arrays are already sorted. Can you get both counts with two pointers and O(1) extra space?
Values are known to be in 1..100. What replaces the hash set?
